claims.text: Controlled changes in deposition parameters can increase reactive-element segregation at grain boundaries in HEA coatings.
Increasing reactive-element segregation enhances grain-boundary chemistry.
Enhanced grain-boundary chemistry stabilizes the nanostructure of HEA coatings.
Inhibiting microcrack initiation improves the wear resistance of HEA coatings.
Substrate temperature and ion flux are deposition variables that can be adjusted to promote reactive-element segregation at grain boundaries.
Modified deposition parameters alter grain-boundary chemistry and the associated phase distribution within a nanocrystalline HEA coating.
Reactive-element segregation stabilizes the grain-boundary network.
A stabilized grain-boundary network reduces localized plastic deformation under sliding contact.
A stabilized grain-boundary network hinders microcrack initiation under sliding contact.
Reduced localized plastic deformation and hindered microcrack initiation lower the overall wear rate.
Coatings deposited under the modified conditions will have lower wear rates than baseline coatings.
Coatings deposited under the modified conditions will have lower microcrack density than baseline coatings.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to nanocrystalline HEA coatings under high-load sliding at moderate temperatures.
Extreme grain growth or non-representative environmental conditions may change the predicted relationship.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant wear-rate reduction after confirming the intended grain-boundary chemical change would falsify the hypothesis.
